description.p: Chronicle builds a complete historical archive of the blogs you follow and merges every article into a single reading queue, ordered by original publication date regardless of which site it came from. It is a way to read a body of writing in the order it was written, rather than in the order you happened to discover it.

Unlike a feed reader, Chronicle is not limited to whatever a site's RSS feed happens to expose. When you add a blog it probes the site and picks the route that recovers the most history: a WordPress REST API, a Ghost content API, a sitemap crawl, or a feed as a last resort. Sites that need special handling can get a purpose-built adapter.

ul.li: It records the original publication date, never the date it discovered an article, and never a later revision date.
Every date carries its provenance and a confidence level, so a date read from a page's dateline is visibly different from one supplied by the publisher.
Precision is kept honestly — a month-precision date is shown as a month, not as a made-up day.
Articles whose date genuinely cannot be determined are collected separately rather than being placed somewhere invented.

description.p: Articles are read inside the application on a typographic reading surface, with headings, lists, quotations, code, tables and images preserved and cached locally so the library keeps working offline. Reading position is remembered per article, and the queue resumes where you left off.
The interface is deliberately minimal: no recommendations, no social features, no gamification. Just the next article. Light and dark palettes follow the desktop preference, or can be set explicitly.

ul.li: Fixed the note box being impossible to type in: letters bound to reading shortcuts (n, j, f, r and the rest) jumped to the next article instead of being typed. Chronicle already stood those shortcuts down while a search box had focus, but could not tell that a note box inside the reading page had it — so the page now says so. Escape leaves the note and saves it, as it did before.
Hovering a link in an article shows where it goes, along the foot of the reading view. Articles are full of links whose text says nothing about their destination.

Hiding read articles no longer empties the Favourites list. Favouriting is something you do to an article while reading it, so almost every favourite is also read — which meant the one list you curate by hand came out empty whenever read articles were hidden. Favourites, like Read, now ignore that setting, and the toggle is shown as inactive there rather than appearing to do nothing.

Notes and highlights. Select any passage while reading to mark it, click a highlight to attach a note to it, and write a note about the article itself at the foot of the reading surface. Both are yours alone — they are never sent anywhere, and an archive update never overwrites them.

Highlights are anchored to the words they mark, not to a position in the file, so they survive a blog editing its post or Chronicle re-fetching it with a better extractor. A highlight whose text genuinely disappears from an article is kept and listed as no longer present, rather than being silently discarded.
Articles carrying a note or a highlight are marked as such in the reading queue.

Updating is now two separate actions, because they are two very different jobs. Fetch new posts collects only what each blog has published since its last update, reading the routes that list the newest posts first and stopping as soon as they reach what is already archived — a routine update that takes seconds. Full archive scan is the old behaviour, re-examining each blog's entire history, and is what you want after adding a blog or to fill gaps.
F5 now fetches new posts; Shift+F5 runs the full scan. Each blog also has both actions on its own row. The command line gains chronicle sync --newest.
Screenshots of the reading view are captured through WebKit's own renderer, fixing captures that came out with the article text missing.

Fixed the library list going blank partway down: a large archive stopped rendering rows past a fixed depth, in every filter. The list is now properly virtualised, so libraries of any size scroll to the end.

Dates printed beside links on a blog's own archive index are now read and used — including compact numeric forms like danluu.com's "08/26", which are interpreted only when the whole listing agrees on a format and comes out in chronological order. Articles already archived with worse dates are corrected from the listing at no request cost.
A dated <time> element now counts whatever its theme happened to name it, fixing sites whose posts carry dates without conventional class names.

Removed the Internet Archive from the pipeline entirely — it was extremely slow and no longer earns its place. The Mr. Money Mustache adapter, which depended on it, is gone too. Adding a site that does not answer at all now says so plainly instead of silently building an empty archive.

Blogs stuck on the retired Internet Archive route are automatically re-detected on their next update — a site that is actually live (fs.blog was) comes back on its proper route, such as its WordPress API, and rebuilds from there.
The blog's own archive listing is now always consulted, with incremental pagination: once a page contains only already-archived posts, the crawl stops there instead of re-walking the whole history.

Discovery now merges every route a blog offers — its feed, its sitemaps (including ones named only in robots.txt), and its own archive pages — instead of picking a single one, so each article carries the best evidence from all of them: the sitemap's completeness with the feed's exact dates and full text.

Updating an already-built archive is now close to free: pages already archived, and pages already examined and judged not to be articles, are no longer refetched — a re-check of a 500-post blog drops from hundreds of requests to a handful.
Posts with no readable publication date are no longer silently dropped: when the feed or the blog's own archive vouches for a page, it is kept and filed under Undated.
A post that has vanished from the live site but still appears in the feed is kept, with the feed's copy of its text.
Articles whose page has permanently gone (404) stop being retried on every update; they become eligible again only when a new route to them appears, such as the Internet Archive.

Sitemap indexes with numbered children (sitemap-1.xml and the like) are now followed instead of being skipped, and clearly non-article children (tag, category, author, image sitemaps) are skipped without being downloaded.
Feeds that keep their history behind pagination (WordPress-style ?paged=, Atom rel="next") are now read all the way back.
Rebuilding a site from the Internet Archive now fetches each snapshot once instead of twice.
Duplicate articles from redirecting URLs are recognised as one article, using the address the page actually lives at.
Adding a blog makes roughly half as many requests, and each blog now remembers where its feed and archive index live (or that it has none) so later updates skip the search.
Fixed "try the Internet Archive" discarding a blog's section scope and feed hints.
Each blog's row now explains, on hover, how its archive is built and what the last update found.
Adding a blog's own archive index (such as a page named /archive/) now recovers its whole history instead of finding nothing, by no longer mistaking that index for a section to scope to.
Pasting a feed URL directly (including a FeedBurner mirror) now detects the site the feed belongs to, so its full archive is built rather than one truncated feed.
A site that is no longer online at all now has its history rebuilt from the Internet Archive automatically.

A site that answers but has no publication dates Chronicle can read no longer waits on a slow Internet Archive search by default — a new button on that blog offers to rebuild from the Internet Archive instead, once the direct routes have actually come up empty.
Reading a blog's full page index (a sitemap or archive listing) is now done several pages at a time instead of one by one, which is much faster for blogs with a large back catalogue.
Updating a blog now shows an estimated time remaining once enough progress has been made to judge it.
Stopping an update is now near-instant, rather than waiting minutes for pages already in flight — this showed up worst against the Internet Archive, whose pages are slow to answer.
Fixed a wrong-date bug where a plain-text heading mentioning an unrelated year (e.g. a subheading like "Lawyers in 1991") could be mistaken for an article's publication date.
Fixed a crash retrieving articles whose URL contains non-ASCII characters, such as a post titled with Greek letters.
Fixed the reading queue silently resetting to the top while scrolled, which happened whenever a background update finished.
Single-key shortcuts no longer fire while typing in the search field.
Opening the library no longer moves focus into the search field.
Adding a blog by a URL with a path now follows only that section of the site, including its pagination.
A single chronological reading queue across every blog you follow, oldest first.
Archive building via WordPress REST, Ghost content API, sitemap crawl or feed, with adapters for sites that need special handling.
Publication dates with precision, confidence and provenance.
Favourites, reading progress and full-text search.
Local image caching for offline reading.
